{{nihongo|'''Shikaumi Shrine'''|志賀海神社}} is a [[shinto shrine]] in the [[Engishiki Jinmyōchō]]. It is located in [[Chikuzen Province]].

'''Shikaumi Shrine''' (しかうみじんじゃ) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|abstract|Q845945|ar|جينجا|arz|ضريح شنتو|bcl|Shinto shrine|ca|Jinja|cs|Šintoistická svatyně|da|Shinto-tempel|de|Shintō-Schrein|el|Σιντοϊστικό Ιερό|eo|Ŝintoa sanktejo|es|Jinja|eu|Jinja|fa|معبد شینتویی|fi|Šintolainen pyhäkkö|fr|Sanctuaire shinto|hi|शिंतो मंदिर|hr|Šintoistički hram|hu|Sintó szentély|id|Jinja|it|Jinja|ja|神社|ka|ძინძია|ko|신사 (신토)|lb|Shintō-Schräin|mr|शिंतो मंदिर|nl|Jinja (heiligdom)|no|Jinja|or|ଜିଞ୍ଜା|pl|Jinja|pt|Templo xintoísta|ru|Дзиндзя|sc|Jinja|simple|Shinto shrine|sl|Šintoistično svetišče|sr|Шинтоистички храм|sv|Jinja|th|ศาลเจ้าชินโต|tok|tomo sewi pi nasin sewi Sinto|tr|Şinto tapınağı|uk|Святилище (синто)|uz|Dzindzya|vi|Thần xã|wuu|神社|zh|神社|zh_yue|神社|qid=Q845945}} located in {{ill|Fukuoka Prefecture|Q123258|qid=Q123258}}{{ill|Fukuoka|Q26600|qid=Q26600}}{{ill|Higashi-ku, Fukuoka|ceb|Higashi Ku (subdistrito sa Hapon, Fukuoka-ken)|cs|Higaši-ku (Fukuoka)|es|Higashi-ku (Fukuoka)|fa|هیگاشی-کو، فوکوئوکا|fi|Higashi-ku (Fukuoka)|fr|Higashi-ku (Fukuoka)|id|Higashi-ku, Fukuoka|it|Higashi-ku (Fukuoka)|ja|東区 (福岡市)|ko|히가시구 (후쿠오카시)|pl|Higashi (Fukuoka)|th|เขตฮิงาชิ (ฟูกูโอกะ)|tr|Higashi, Fukuoka|ur|ہیگاشی وارڈ، فوکوکا|vi|Higashi, Fukuoka|zh|東區 (福岡市)|zh_yue|東區 (福岡市)|qid=Q1206659|lt=Higashi Ward}}{{ill|Shika Island|Q3077260|qid=Q3077260}}. It is a {{ill|Shikinaisha|fr|Shikinaisha|zh|式內社|qid=Q134917286|lt=Shikinaisha}} ({{ill|Myōjin Taisha|Q9610964|qid=Q9610964}}). Under the {{ill|Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|Q712534|Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|lt=former shrine ranking}}, it was classified as a {{ill|Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|Q712534|Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|lt=Kanpei-shōsha}}, and today it is a {{ill|Beppyo shrine|ja|別表神社|mr|बेप्प्यो तीर्थ|simple|Beppyo shrine|zh|別表神社|qid=Q10898274}} of the {{ill|Association of Shinto Shrines|Q908077|qid=Q908077}}.

It claims to be the head shrine of all {{ill|Watatsumi shrines|Q11607434|qid=Q11607434}} and {{ill|Watatsumi Shrine (disambiguation)|Q123530063|qid=Q123530063}} nationwide<ref name="由緒書"/>. It is praised as the “capital of dragons” and is known as a place associated with the ancient clan {{ill|Azumi people|Q3377806|qid=Q3377806}} (also written Adzumi).

=== Shrine name ===  
Regarding the origin of the word “Shika” (志賀), which is also the island name of {{ill|Shika Island|Q3077260|qid=Q3077260}}, an excerpt from the *Chikuzen no Kuni Fudoki* <ref group="原">Excerpt from the *Chikuzen no Kuni Fudoki* cited in *Shaku Nihongi*, vol. 6, section on the deities worshiped by the Azumi no Muraji, etc.</ref> says that, based on a tradition connected to {{ill|Empress Jingū|Q232803|qid=Q232803}}’s expedition to {{ill|Silla|Q28456|qid=Q28456}}, the area was called “Chikashima (近島, ‘near island’),” which later shifted in pronunciation to “Shikashima (資珂島)” <ref name="地名"/>.  

The shrine name “Shikaumi” (志賀海) is now pronounced “Shikaumi,” but as for the original pronunciation there are various theories such as “Shika no Wata,” “Shika no Ama,” “Shika no Umi,” and “Shika ni Imasu Wata,” among others <ref name="神々"/>.  

=== Enshrined deities ===  
The deities are enshrined as follows: one principal deity in each of the left, center, and right halls, along with one associated deity in each hall <ref name="由緒書"/>. The three principal deities are collectively called the “{{ill|Watatsumi|abstract|Q1474187|az|Vatatsumi|de|Watatsumi|es|Watatsumi|fa|واتاتسومی|fr|Watatsumi|hu|Vatacumi|ja|ワタツミ|ko|와타쓰미|mni|ꯋꯇꯠꯁꯨꯃꯤ|pl|Watatsumi|ru|Ватацуми|simple|Watatsumi|uk|Вататсумі|zh|綿津見|qid=Q1474187|lt=Watatsumi Three Deities}}” (綿津見三神, watatsumi sanshin) <ref name="由緒書"/>.  
* Left Hall: **Nakatsu Watatsumi no Kami** (仲津綿津見神)  
** Associated deity of the Left Hall: {{ill|Empress Jingū|Q232803|qid=Q232803}} (神功皇后)  
* Center Hall: **Sokotsu Watatsumi no Kami** (底津綿津見神)  
** Associated deity of the Center Hall: {{ill|Tamayori-hime (mother of Jimmu)|Q3082751|qid=Q3082751|lt=Princess Tamayorihime}} (玉依姫命)  
* Right Hall: **Uwatsu Watatsumi no Kami** (表津綿津見神)   
** Associated deity of the Right Hall: {{ill|Emperor Ōjin|Q317997|qid=Q317997}} (応神天皇)  

=== About the enshrined deities ===  
The three Watatsumi (sea / Watatsumi / Watatsumi of the “少童” reading) deities are regarded as sea gods, as seen in the ancient name for the sea “Wata / Watanohara” (“sea = wata, watanohara”) <ref>“Kaijin Shinkō” entry, *Kokushi Daijiten*.</ref>. In the “birth of the gods” section of the {{ill|Kojiki|ace|Kojiki|ar|كوجيكي|az|Kociki|bcl|Kojiki|be|Кодзікі|bg|Коджики|ca|Kojiki|ckb|کۆجیکی|cs|Kodžiki|da|Kojiki|de|Kojiki|eo|Koĝiki|es|Kojiki|et|Kojiki|eu|Kojiki|fa|کوجیکی|fi|Kojiki|fr|Kojiki|gl|Kojiki|he|קוג'יקי|hi|कोजिकी|hr|Kojiki|hu|Kodzsiki|hy|Կոձիկի|id|Kojiki|it|Kojiki|ja|古事記|ka|კოძიკი|kk|Кодзики|kn|ಕೋಜಿಕಿ|ko|고사기|la|Kojiki|lt|Kodžiki|mk|Коџики|ml|കൊജികി|ms|Kojiki|my|ခိုဂျိခိ|nl|Kojiki|no|Kojiki|oc|Kojiki|pl|Kojiki|pt|Kojiki|ro|Kojiki|rsk|Кодїки|ru|Кодзики|sh|Kojiki|simple|Kojiki|sk|Kodžiki|sl|Kodžiki|sr|Коџики|sv|Kojiki|ta|கோஜிகி|th|โคจิกิ|tl|Kojiki|tr|Kojiki|uk|Кодзікі|vi|Cổ sự ký|zh|古事記|zh_classical|古事記|qid=Q813031}} and {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ar|نيهون شوكي|as|নিহন শ্ব'কি|az|Nihon şoki|bcl|Nihon Shoki|bg|Нихоншоки|ca|Nihon Shoki|cs|Nihonšoki|de|Nihonshoki|el|Νιχόν Σόκι|eo|Nihon Ŝoki|es|Nihonshoki|eu|Nihon Shoki|fa|نیهون شوکی|fi|Nihonshoki|fr|Nihon shoki|gl|Nihon Shoki|he|ניהון שוקי|hi|निहोन शोकी|hr|Nihon Shoki|hu|Nihonsoki|id|Nihon Shoki|it|Nihon shoki|ja|日本書紀|jv|Nihon Shoki|ko|일본서기|la|Nihon Shoki|mk|Нихон шоки|ms|Nihon Shoki|my|နိဟွန်းရှောခိ|nl|Nihon Shoki|no|Nihonshoki|oc|Nihon shoki|pl|Nihon-shoki|pt|Nihon Shoki|rsk|Нихон Шоки|ru|Нихон сёки|sco|Nihon Shoki|sh|Nihon Shoki|simple|Nihon Shoki|sl|Nihon Šoki|sq|Nihon Shoki|sr|Нихон шоки|sv|Nihonshoki|ta|நிஹான் ஷோகி|th|นิฮงโชกิ|tl|Nihon Shoki|tr|Nihon Shoki|uk|Ніхон Сьокі|uz|Nihon shoki|vi|Nhật Bản thư kỷ|zh|日本書紀|zh_min_nan|Ji̍t-pún Su-kì|zh_yue|日本書紀|qid=Q813935}}, during the purification rite ({{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=misogi}}), they are described as gods born together with the {{ill|Sumiyoshi sanjin|Q1114013|qid=Q1114013}} as follows.  
* *Kojiki*  
*: It calls the three born deities—Sokotsu Watatsumi no Kami, Nakatsu Watatsumi no Kami, and Uwatsu Watatsumi no Kami—collectively “Watatsumi no Kami,” and states, “They are the gods whom the Azumi no Muraji (あずみのむらじ) and others venerate as their ancestral deity” <ref name="綿津見神"/>.  
* *Nihon Shoki*  
*: After saying, “The sea gods born were named Sukunahiko no Mikoto,” it records that the three born deities—Sokotsu Sukunahiko no Mikoto, Nakatsu Sukunahiko no Mikoto, and Uwatsu Sukunahiko no Mikoto—are “the gods whom the Azumi no Muraji and others worship” <ref name="綿津見神"/>.  

Thus, in the *Kojiki* and *Nihon Shoki*, the Watatsumi Three Deities are treated as the ancestral gods or worshiped gods of the **{{ill|Azumi people|Q3377806|qid=Q3377806}}** (Azumi-uji/Azumi-uji; also written 安曇氏, 阿曇族, 安曇族) <ref name="地名"/>. The reading “Azumi/Azumi” is also seen as an abbreviation of “Amatsumi (海津見),” and the Azumi clan who served these deities were a *tomonomiyatsuko* clan that oversaw groups of seafaring people <ref name="綿津見神">“Watatsumi no Kami” entry, *Kokushi Daijiten*.</ref>.  

In the {{ill|Kujiki|Q2716751|qid=Q2716751}} <ref group="原">*Sendai Kujihongi*, “Onmyō Hongi” (see [{{NDLDC|991097/110}} *Kokushi Taikei*, vol. 7] (Keizai Zasshisha, 1897–1901; National Diet Library Digital Collection), frame 110).</ref>, likewise in the section on the birth of the gods, it says: “The three Sukunahiko deities are worshiped by the Azumi no Muraji and others; they are the Tsukushi Shika gods,” <ref name="神々"/> and Shikaumi Shrine is named as a clan deity under the title “Tsukushi Shika no Kami (筑紫斯香神)” <ref name="神々"/>.  

As other major sea gods besides Watatsumi, Sumiyoshi ({{ill|Sumiyoshi sanjin|Q1114013|qid=Q1114013}}; worshiped by the Sumiyoshi clan) and Munakata ({{ill|Three Munakata Goddesses|Q10948069|qid=Q10948069}}; worshiped by the {{ill|Munakata clan|Q16481907|qid=Q16481907|lt=Munakata lineage}}) are well known, and in northern Kyūshū there are shrines dedicated to each: {{ill|Sumiyoshi Shrine (Fukuoka)|abstract|Q29682|de|Sumiyoshi-Schrein (Fukuoka)|fr|Sumiyoshi-jinja (Fukuoka)|ja|住吉神社 (福岡市)|simple|Sumiyoshi Shrine (Fukuoka)|zh|住吉神社 (福岡市)|qid=Q29682|lt=Sumiyoshi Shrine}} and {{ill|Munakata Taisha|Q704962|qid=Q704962}}.  

=== History ===  
[[File:Shikanoshima Island, enkei.jpg|thumb|220px|right|{{center|{{ill|Shika Island|Q3077260|qid=Q3077260}}, where Shikaumi Shrine is located}}]]  

=== Founding ===  
The founding date is unknown <ref name="由緒書"/>. According to shrine tradition, in ancient times it consisted of three shrines on Katsuma Beach on the north side of {{ill|Shika Island|Q3077260|qid=Q3077260}}: Uwatsu-gū, Nakatsu-gū, and Okitsu-gū; but {{ill|Azumi-no-isora|Q1755974|qid=Q1755974}} (Azumi no Isora: ancestor of the {{ill|Azumi people|Q3377806|qid=Q3377806}}) relocated the Uwatsu-gū to the south side of Shikanoshima, making it the present precinct <ref name="由緒書"/>. Nakatsu-gū and Okitsu-gū are now subordinate shrines <ref name="由緒書"/>. Azumi no Isora is also said to have served as helmsman in {{ill|Empress Jingū|Q232803|qid=Q232803}}’s expedition to {{ill|Silla|Q28456|qid=Q28456}} <ref name="由緒書"/><ref name="神々"/>.  

In ancient northern Kyūshū, the {{ill|Azumi people|Q3377806|qid=Q3377806}} (also written 安曇氏), who governed sea people ({{ill|Ama (diving)|Q1577970|qid=Q1577970}}), are said to have controlled maritime routes <ref name="角川"/>. Shikanoshima was a key point for sea traffic, and the area including Shikanoshima and {{ill|Umi no Nakamichi|ceb|Uminonakamichi|fr|Umino Nakamichi|ja|海の中道|ko|우미노나카미치|zh|海之中道|qid=Q2404998}} <ref group="注">Considered the area of Shika-gō and Azumi-gō in Kasuya District of Chikuzen Province as seen in the *Wamyōshō* (from the *Dictionary of Personal Names of Ancient Japanese Clans*, entry on the Azumi clan). Shika-gō is identified with Shikanoshima; Azumi-gō is identified with the area from Kamiwajiro and Shimowajiro in Higashi Ward, Fukuoka City to Shingū Town in Kasuya District, or with Shikanoshima (from *Place Names of Fukuoka Prefecture*, entries on Shika-gō and Azumi-gō).</ref> is said to have been the Azumi clan’s home base <ref name="角川">*Kadokawa Nihon Chimei Daijiten*, entry on Shikaumi Shrine.</ref>, and Shikaumi Shrine is thought to have been the clan’s central shrine <ref name="地名"/>. Even today, all of Shikanoshima is regarded as a sacred precinct <ref>*Kadokawa Nihon Chimei Daijiten*, entry on Shikanoshima.</ref>, and the current priestly family also claims descent from the Azumi clan <ref name="角川"/>. The Azumi clan is said to have expanded throughout Japan, and place names such as “Shika” and “Atsumi”—for example {{ill|Azumino|Q534667|qid=Q534667}} in {{ill|Nagano Prefecture|Q127877|qid=Q127877}}, {{ill|Shika, Ishikawa|Q1349406|qid=Q1349406}} in {{ill|Hakui District, Ishikawa|Q1130953|qid=Q1130953}} of {{ill|Ishikawa Prefecture|Q131281|qid=Q131281}}, the {{ill|Ado Shikanoshima is also known for the discovery of the gold seal ({{ill|King of Na gold seal|Q2975212|qid=Q2975212}}), but it is unclear why the seal of {{ill|Nakoku|Q600473|qid=Q600473}} was found there. Some theories speculate a connection between the Azumi clan—and by extension Shikaumi Shrine as their clan deity—and Na, and at Najima Shrine in Najima, Higashi Ward, Fukuoka City, the Azumi clan is regarded as the “Nake-nushi” <ref>{{Cite web|和書|url=https://lunabura.exblog.jp/14132415/|title=Najima Shrine|accessdate=April 13, 2010|publisher=Ayasugi Luna}}</ref>.  

=== Overview history ===  
In surviving records, there is mention in the “Sumiyoshi Taisha Shige (Sumiyoshi Taisha Jindaiki)”—dated Tenpyō 3 ({{ill|731|Q23566|qid=Q23566}}), though likely compiled around the early {{ill|Heian period|ar|فترة هييآن|ast|Periodu Heian|az|Heyan dövrü|bcl|Panahon ni Heian|bg|Хеян|bn|হেইআন যুগ|br|Marevezh Heian|ca|Període Heian|cs|Období Heian|de|Heian-Zeit|el|Περίοδος Χεϊάν|eo|Epoko Heian|es|Período Heian|eu|Heian aroa|fa|دوره هی‌آن|fi|Heian-kausi|fr|Époque de Heian|gl|Período Heian|he|תקופת הייאן|hi|हेआन काल|hr|Heian (razdoblje)|hu|Heian-kor|hy|Հեիան ժամանակաշրջան|id|Zaman Heian|it|Periodo Heian|ja|平安時代|ka|ჰეიანის პერიოდი|ko|헤이안 시대|la|Aevum Heian|lt|Hejano laikotarpis|mn|Хэйан|mr|हियन कालावधी|ms|Zaman Heian|my|ဟဲအိအန်ခေတ်|nl|Heianperiode|nn|Heian|no|Heian-perioden|oc|Epòca d'Heian|pl|Heian|ps|هېيان دوره|pt|Período Heian|ro|Perioada Heian|ru|Период Хэйан|sh|Heianski period|simple|Heian period|sk|Obdobie Heian|sl|Obdobje Heian|sq|Periudha Heian|sr|Хеиан период|sv|Heian|ta|ஹையன் காலகட்டம்|th|ยุคเฮอัง|tl|Panahong Heian|tr|Heian Dönemi|uk|Період Хейан|vi|Thời kỳ Heian|war|Panahon Heian|wuu|平安时代|zh|平安时代|zh_classical|平安朝|zh_min_nan|Heian sî-tāi|zh_yue|平安時代|qid=Q193292}}—of “Naka District Azumi Shrine, three offerings” and “Shika Shrine” <ref name="地名"/>. Also, in the {{ill|Shinshō Kyakuchokufushō|Q11502312|qid=Q11502312}} <ref group="原">*Shinshō Kakuchokufushō* 10, “Shinji Shoke Fuko,” directive of Daidō 1 (806) (see {{Harvnb|Shintō / Shrine Historical Sources Compilation}}).</ref>, it appears that as of {{ill|Daidō|Q1373191|qid=Q1373191|lt=Daidō}} 1 ({{ill|806|Q30021|qid=Q30021}}), “Azumi no Kami” had eight households as *shinpu* (donated *fuko*) <ref name="地名"/>.  

According to national histories, in {{ill|Ten'an|Q1075611|qid=Q1075611|lt=Ten’an}} 3 ({{ill|859|Q23897|qid=Q23897}}) <ref group="原" name="貞観"/> the divine rank (*shinkai*) of “Shikaumi no Kami” was raised to Junior Fifth Rank, Upper Grade, and in {{ill|Gangyō|Q747451|qid=Q747451}} 4 ({{ill|880|Q23618|qid=Q23618}}) <ref group="原" name="賀津万"/> “Katsuma no Kami” (identified with Nakatsu-gū) was raised to Junior Fifth Rank, Lower Grade <ref name="地名"/>.  

In the “Register of Deities” (*Jinmyōchō*) of the {{ill|Engishiki|ar|إنجيشيكي (كتاب ياباني)|de|Engishiki|es|Engishiki|fr|Engishiki|he|אנגישיקי|id|Engishiki|it|Engishiki|ja|延喜式|ko|엔기시키|min|Engishiki|mr|इंगिशिकी|nl|Engishiki|pt|Engishiki|ru|Энгисики|simple|Engishiki|tr|Engishiki|uk|Енґісікі|zh|延喜式|qid=Q1342448}} compiled in {{ill|Enchō|Q1327274|qid=Q1327274|lt=Enchō}} 5 ({{ill|927|Q30470|qid=Q30470}}), it is listed under Naka District of {{ill|Chikuzen Province|cs|Provincie Čikuzen|de|Provinz Chikuzen|es|Provincia de Chikuzen|fa|ولایت چیکوزن|fr|Chikuzen|gl|Provincia de Chikuzen|id|Provinsi Chikuzen|it|Chikuzen (provincia)|ja|筑前国|ko|지쿠젠국|lt|Čikudzeno žemė|nl|Chikuzen (provincie)|no|Chikuzen (provins)|pt|Província de Chikuzen|ru|Тикудзэн (провинция)|simple|Chikuzen Province|sk|Čikuzen (provincia)|sr|Провинција Чикузен|tr|Chikuzen (vilayet)|uk|Провінція Тікудзен|zh|筑前國|zh_min_nan|Tikuzen-kok|zh_yue|筑前國|qid=Q1047664}} as “Shikaumi Shrine, three seats, all Myōjin Taisha,” and is ranked as a {{ill|Myōjin Taisha|Q9610964|qid=Q9610964}} <ref name="角川"/>.  

Other Heian and Kamakura-period sources concerning Shikaumi Shrine are few <ref name="角川"/>; in the {{ill|Shōyūki|Q11459316|qid=Q11459316}} <ref group="原">*Shōyūki*, entries for August 27 and August 30, Manju 4 (1027).</ref>, there is a note that in {{ill|Manju (era)|Q1194155|qid=Q1194155}} 3 ({{ill|1026|Q19269|qid=Q19269}}) the shrine’s priest traveled to {{ill|Song dynasty|Q7462|qid=Q7462}} (entered Song) and returned the following year <ref name="地名"/>.  

[[File:Mōko Shūrai Ekotoba e20(2).JPG|thumb|200px|right|{{center|Torii and shrine buildings depicted in the {{ill|Mōko Shūrai Ekotoba|Q3087790|qid=Q3087790}}}}]]  
In the {{ill|Kamakura period|Q236205|qid=Q236205}}, during the {{ill|Mongol invasions of Japan|Q208156|qid=Q208156}}, Shikanoshima became a battlefield, but Shikaumi Shrine’s precinct is recorded in the *Mōko Shūrai Ekotoba* under the name “Shikanoshima Daimyōjin” <ref name="地名"/>.  

From the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|Q264012|qid=Q264012}} onward, Shikaumi Shrine came strongly under warrior control <ref name="地名"/>. In {{ill|Ōnin|Q1143903|qid=Q1143903}} 3 ({{ill|1469|Q6566|qid=Q6566}}), Shōni Yoritada confirmed the office of Shikanoshima’s chief priest for the abbot of Tōgetsuji on Tsushima <ref name="地名"/>, and afterward it received patronage from the {{ill|Ōuchi clan|Q1348909|qid=Q1348909}} <ref name="角川"/>. It is also said that before sailing to {{ill|Ming dynasty|Q9903|qid=Q9903}}, people prayed here for safe voyages <ref name="地名"/>.  

In the early modern era, it received protection from the {{ill|Kobayakawa clan|Q2975298|qid=Q2975298}} and {{ill|Kuroda clan|Q2975305|qid=Q2975305}} who ruled Chikuzen Province <ref name="角川"/>. It is said that {{ill|Kuroda Nagamasa|Q950496|qid=Q950496}}, who entered the province in {{ill|Keichō|Q1328185|qid=Q1328185}} 5 ({{ill|1600|Q6720|qid=Q6720}}), built the main sanctuary, worship hall, rōmon gate, and other structures <ref name="地名"/>. In {{ill|Bunka|Q1373146|qid=Q1373146|lt=Bunka}} 14 ({{ill|1817|Q6958|qid=Q6958}}), the shrine lands amounted to 50 koku <ref name="地名"/>.  

In {{ill|Meiji era|Q3125096|qid=Q3125096}} 5 ({{ill|1872|Q7753|qid=Q7753}}), under the modern shrine ranking system, it was designated a village shrine, and in {{ill|Taishō era|Q329174|qid=Q329174}} 15 ({{ill|1926|Q5259|qid=Q5259}}) it was promoted to *Kanpei Shōsha* <ref name="神々">“Shikaumi Shrine” entry, *Nihon no Kamigami*.</ref>.  

=== Divine ranks ===  
* {{ill|Ten'an|Q1075611|qid=Q1075611|lt=Ten’an}} 3 ({{ill|859|Q23897|qid=Q23897}}) January 27: Shikaumi no Kami from Junior Fifth Rank, Lower Grade to Junior Fifth Rank, Upper Grade (*Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku*) <ref group="原" name="貞観">*Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku*, entry for January 27, Jōgan 1 (859) (see {{Harvnb|Shintō / Shrine Historical Sources Compilation}}).</ref>  
* {{ill|Gangyō|Q747451|qid=Q747451}} 4 ({{ill|880|Q23618|qid=Q23618}}) March 22: Katsuma no Kami from Senior Sixth Rank, Upper Grade to Junior Fifth Rank, Lower Grade (*Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku*) <ref group="原" name="賀津万">*Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku*, entry for March 22, Gangyō 4 (880).</ref> — From the divine name “Katsuma (賀津万),” identified with the subordinate shrine Nakatsu-gū (Katsuma Myōjin) <ref name="地名">*Place Names of Fukuoka Prefecture*, entry on Shikaumi Shrine.</ref>.  

=== Precincts ===  
[[File:Shikaumi-jinja shaden.JPG|thumb|200px|right|{{center|Worship hall (front) and main sanctuary (rear right)}}]]  
The precinct is located on the south side of Shikanoshima. It is said that Shikaumi Shrine was formerly on the north side of Shikanoshima and consisted of three shrines—Uwatsu-gū, Nakatsu-gū, and Okitsu-gū <ref name="由緒書"/>. Of these, Uwatsu-gū was transferred here and became the present main shrine, while Nakatsu-gū and Okitsu-gū are now subordinate shrines. The former site of Uwatsu-gū is said to be in Katsuma, Higashi Ward, Fukuoka City ({{Coord|33|41|13.00|N|130|17|32.74|E|region:JP-40_type:landmark|name=Site of Uwatsu-gū (former location)}}).  

In the precinct’s Rokkakudō (鹿角堂), many deer antlers—said to number over ten thousand—have been dedicated. There is also a sacred stone dedicated in later times called the “Kameishi (亀石, ‘turtle stone’),” linked to a tradition that during {{ill|Empress Jingū|Q232803|qid=Q232803}}’s {{ill|Three Han Campaign|Q11249435|qid=Q11249435}}, {{ill|Azumi-no-isora|Q1755974|qid=Q1755974}} appeared before the empress riding a turtle <ref name="神々"/>.  

Along the approach stands a stone *Hōkyōintō* pagoda. A {{ill|Hōkyōintō|Q3146365|qid=Q3146365}} is a pagoda that enshrines a Buddhist scripture (the *Hōkyōin Dharani Sutra*) <ref name="説明板">Explanatory signboard in the precinct.</ref>. This one bears an inscription from {{ill|Jōwa (Muromachi period)|Q1146143|qid=Q1146143|lt=Jōwa}} 3 ({{ill|1347|Q6082|qid=Q6082}}) in the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|Q264012|qid=Q264012}}, and is the oldest complete example in Fukuoka Prefecture <ref name="説明板"/>. Made of {{ill|Granite|Q41177|qid=Q41177}}, it consists of a base, body, roof, and finial, with a total height of 334.5 cm <ref name="説明板"/>. It is designated a tangible cultural property of Fukuoka Prefecture <ref name="塔"/>.  

The first torii was built in {{ill|Kanbun (era)|Q1146228|qid=Q1146228}} 10 ({{ill|1670|Q7606|qid=Q7606}}) by {{ill|Kuroda Mitsuyuki|Q11678571|qid=Q11678571}}, the third lord of the {{ill|Fukuoka Domain|Q208766|qid=Q208766}} <ref name="地名"/>. The next torii was built in {{ill|Genroku|Q1325001|qid=Q1325001}} 13 ({{ill|1700|Q6813|qid=Q6813}}), and the torii by the seashore was built in An’ei 3 ({{ill|1774|Q7697|qid=Q7697}}) <ref name="地名"/>.

=== Auxiliary shrines (sessha and massha) ===  
There are a total of 24 auxiliary shrines: 5 sessha and 19 massha <ref name="由緒書">Shrine origin pamphlet. </ref>. According to the *Chikuzen no Kuni Zoku Fudoki*, there were once 375 massha, but they were damaged in the Warring States turmoil; at the time of restoration by {{ill|Mochiyo Ōuchi|Q11432525|qid=Q11432525}} in {{ill|Eikyō|Q1193059|qid=Q1193059}} 11 ({{ill|1439|Q6380|qid=Q6380}}), there were a little over 120, and later in the Edo period there were only about five <ref name="神々"/>.  

=== Sessha ===  
[[File:Okitsujima Island near Shikanoshima Island 5.jpg|thumb|200px|{{center|{{ill|Okitsujima|Q49665728|qid=Q49665728}}, where Okitsu-gū is enshrined}}]]

* Okitsu-gū (沖津宮)  
** Location: Katsuma, Higashi Ward, Fukuoka City ({{Coord|33|41|20.12|N|130|17|25.07|E|region:JP-40_type:landmark|name=Sessha: Okitsu-gū}})  
** Enshrined deities: Uwatsu Watatsumi no Kami, {{ill|Ame-no-Minakanushi|Q2842779|qid=Q2842779|lt=Ame no Minakanushi no Kami}}  
* Nakatsu-gū (仲津宮 / 中津宮)  
** Location: Katsuma, Higashi Ward, Fukuoka City ({{Coord|33|41|11.80|N|130|17|27.45|E|region:JP-40_type:landmark|name=Sessha: Nakatsu-gū}})  
** Enshrined deity: Nakatsu Watatsumi no Kami  
*: Also called “Katsuma Myōjin,” and identified with “Katsuma no Kami” in the {{ill|Kokushi genzaisha|Q118304363|qid=Q118304363}} <ref group="原" name="賀津万"/> <ref name="地名"/>.  
*: In {{ill|Heisei era|Q234510|qid=Q234510}} 6 ({{ill|1994|Q2067|qid=Q2067}}), a kofun (Nakatsu-gū Kofun) was discovered in the forecourt area <ref name="中津宮古墳">[http://bunkazai.city.fukuoka.lg.jp/cultural_properties/detail/481 Nakatsu-gū Kofun] (Fukuoka City Economic Tourism and Culture Bureau, “Cultural Properties of Fukuoka City”).</ref>. Because it was damaged by shrine construction, its size and form are unclear, but grave goods were found along with a pit-type stone chamber <ref name="中津宮古墳"/>. It is dated to the first half of the {{ill|7th century|Q8089|qid=Q8089}} and is regarded as the tomb of a leader of the local maritime group <ref name="中津宮古墳"/>.

=== Massha ===  
There are 19 massha in total: 12 in Shika, 5 in Katsuma, 1 in Hiro, and 1 in Ōtake <ref name="由緒書"/>.

=== Festivals ===  
=== Annual grand festival ===  
Shikaumi Shrine’s annual grand festival is called the “Kunchi Festival” (国土祭). On the previous day, every other year (odd-numbered years in the Western calendar), the shrine’s largest festival, the “Goshinkō Festival” (御神幸祭), is held <ref name="神幸"/>. In the past it was held on the old lunar calendar: September 8 (Goshinkō Festival) and September 9 (Kunchi Festival), but today it is held on {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Health and Sports Day}} and the day before (the second Monday of October and the preceding day) <ref name="神幸"/>.  

Before the festival, on lunar September 1 (October 1), a “Otokoyama Festival” is held in which a {{ill|demarchy|Q5433694|qid=Q5433694}} determines whether to conduct the procession (today it is held biennially) <ref name="神幸"/>. In the Goshinkō Festival, beginning at 9 p.m. on the night of lunar September 8 (the night before Health and Sports Day), three mikoshi (Ichinoto, Ninoto, Sannotō) depart and proceed to a temporary shrine (tonomiya) <ref name="神幸"/>. There, performances based on the shrine’s origin traditions—such as the “Dragon Dance,” “Yaotome Dance,” and “Kakko Dance”—are dedicated <ref name="神幸"/>. The mikoshi then return to the shrine, the spirit is transferred back to the main sanctuary, and the Goshinkō Festival ends <ref name="神幸"/>. On the following day, lunar September 9 (Health and Sports Day), *yabusame* ({{ill|Yabusame|Q1886157|qid=Q1886157}}) is offered <ref name="神幸"/>.  

Because it involves moving the divine spirit at night and aims to reaffirm the tradition for the people through performances rooted in the shrine’s origin narrative, the Goshinkō Festival is said to preserve an ancient form <ref name="神幸"/>. The rites are designated a Fukuoka Prefecture intangible folk cultural property as the “Shikaumi Shrine Shinkō Event” <ref name="神幸"/>.  

=== Special rites ===  
; Hosha Festival  
: “Hosha-sai.” A New Year rite held among annual events from January 2 to 15, conducted on a Sunday near January 15 <ref name="歩射"/>. In the past, Hosha was held on January 15 <ref name="歩射"/>. “Hosha,” i.e., shooting a {{ill|Bow and arrow|Q19827042|qid=Q19827042|lt=bow}} on foot (not on horseback), is a Shinto rite for warding off evil and divining the year’s fortunes <ref name="歩射"/>. It is connected to a tradition of Azumi Momotari (百足) slaying an earth spider (tsuchigumo) <ref name="歩射"/>.  
: In Hosha, young men chosen from parishioners serve as archers and shoot at a large target set up along the approach <ref name="歩射"/>. Preparations begin on January 2 and proceed through various rituals, forming a traditional rite <ref name="歩射"/>. It is designated a Fukuoka Prefecture intangible folk cultural property as the “Shikaumi Shrine Hosha Festival” <ref name="歩射"/>.  
; Yamahome Tanemaki Gyoryō-sai / Yamahome Gyoryō-sai  
: Also called the “Yamahome Festival.” The spring Yamahome Tanemaki Gyoryō-sai is held on April 15, and the autumn Yamahome Gyoryō-sai on November 15 <ref name="山ほめ"/>. Formerly they were held on lunar February 15 and November 15 and were called the “Hunting and Fishing Festival” <ref name="山ほめ"/>. The spring rite includes gestures of sowing to pray for a good harvest, while the autumn rite includes gestures of hauling nets to pray for a bountiful catch.  
: Next, the three Shika mountains (Katsuyama, Kinugasa-yama, and Mikasa-yama) are purified and praised (yamahome) <ref name="山ほめ"/>. Then gestures of shooting a deer (hunting rite) and catching sea bream (fishing rite) are performed <ref name="山ほめ"/>. It is designated a Fukuoka Prefecture intangible folk cultural property as the “Yamahome Festival” <ref name="山ほめ"/>.  
: As a {{ill|kagura uta|Q11590393|qid=Q11590393}}, the following song is sung <ref>[http://www.sikanosima.jp/event-maturi/yamafome08/index2.html Yamahome Gyoryō Festival] (personal website).</ref>.  
{{Cquote|<small>Kimigayo<dai> wa / chiyo ni yachiyo ni / sazareishi no / iwao to narite koke no musu made<br />Are haya / are koso wa / wagakimi no mifune kaya / utsurōgase migai ni inochi / senzai to iu<br />Hana koso / saitara / oki no onzu no shiohaya ni haetaram tsuruo ni kuwazaram / tai wa oki no murendai hoya<br /><br />Shika no hama / nagaki o mireba / ikuyo heranamu / Kashii-ji ni muita ru ano fukiage no hama / chiyo ni yachiyo made<br />Koyoi yowa ni tsuki tamau / mifune koso / taga mifune arikeru yo / are haya / are koso wa / Azumi no kimi no meshi tamau / mifune ni narikeru yo<br />Iruka yo / iruka / shiohaya no iruka / Isora ga saki ni / tai tsuru okina</small>|20px||Yamahome Festival Kagura Song}}  
It closely resembles “{{ill|Kimigayo|Q81534|qid=Q81534}},” Japan’s {{ill|National anthem|Q23691|qid=Q23691}}, but according to Kinoshita Mishige (father of Kinoshita Norio, former chief priest of {{ill|Kashii-gū|Q631373|qid=Q631373}}), records of Tsukushi kagura once held at Kashii Shrine show that this Yamahome Festival kagura song spread via traveling performers, was included in the *Kokin Wakashū*, later became the “Kimigayo” found in the Satsuma biwa piece “Hōraisan,” and then became the national anthem.  

It is also said that similar kagura songs are transmitted at Najima Shrine in Higashi Ward, Fukuoka City, and at {{ill|Furogu Shrine|Q11282543|qid=Q11282543}} in {{ill|Ōkawa, Fukuoka|Q385248|qid=Q385248}}, {{ill|Fukuoka Prefecture|Q123258|qid=Q123258}} (the priests of the three shrines—Shikaumi, Najima, and Fūromiya—are all of the Azumi lineage).  
; Tanabata Festival  
: A festival held from August 6 to 7 praying for safe fishing and a good catch <ref name="七夕"/>. Formerly it was held on lunar July 7 <ref name="七夕">[http://bunkazai.city.fukuoka.lg.jp/cultural_properties/detail/123 Tanabata Festival of Shikaumi Shrine] (Fukuoka City Economic Tourism and Culture Bureau, “Cultural Properties of Fukuoka City”).</ref>.  
: During the festival, fishermen of Hakata Bay visit the port on boats flying big-catch flags, then worship at Shikaumi Shrine <ref name="七夕"/>. The festival is also mentioned in Kaibara Ekken’s *Chikuzen no Kuni Zoku Fudoki*, and it is said that in earlier times there were many stalls <ref name="七夕"/>.  
; Otokoyama Festival  
: A rite held on October 1 to decide by {{ill|demarchy|Q5433694|qid=Q5433694}} whether the year’s grand festival will include a procession <ref name="神幸"/>. Formerly it was held on lunar September 1 <ref name="神幸"/>. However, today the procession is conducted biennially <ref name="神幸"/>.  

=== Cultural properties ===  
=== Important Cultural Property (national designation) ===  
* Gilded bell (鍍金鐘) (craft)  
*: A {{ill|Bonshō|Q8192099|qid=Q8192099}} (Korean bell) transmitted at Shikaumi Shrine, retaining traces of gilding (“tokin” meaning plating) on its surface. Though small (height 52.8 cm; mouth diameter 30.5 cm), it is characterized by a relatively large dragon handle at the top. The upper and lower bands bear peony arabesque patterns, and four striking pads with sixteen-petaled lotus designs are placed slightly above the lower band. Four seated Buddha images are cast on the bell body, with two heavenly guardian figures beneath each. The bell is unsigned, but its form resembles the Korean bell at {{ill|Mandara-ji Temple|Q11515245|qid=Q11515245}} in {{ill|Kōnan, Aichi|Q820496|qid=Q820496}}, which bears a date corresponding to 1234 CE, and it is thought to date to the early 13th century in the {{ill|Goryeo|Q28208|qid=Q28208}} period <ref name="坪井">Ryohei Tsuboi, *Revised: Bonshō and Ancient Culture* (Business Education Publishing, 1993), pp. 302–304.</ref>. Deposited at the {{ill|Fukuoka City Museum|Q11592224|qid=Q11592224}}. Designated April 14, 1906 (Meiji 39).  

=== Fukuoka Prefecture-designated cultural properties ===  
* Tangible cultural properties  
** Stone Hōkyōintō pagoda (archaeological material) <ref name="塔">[http://bunkazai.city.fukuoka.lg.jp/cultural_properties/detail/323 Stone Hōkyōintō Pagoda] (Fukuoka City Economic Tourism and Culture Bureau, “Cultural Properties of Fukuoka City”).</ref> — Designated October 29, 1958 (Shōwa 33).  
** Fragmentary mold for a slender bronze sword (archaeological material)  
**: A casting mold for a {{ill|Slender bronze dagger|Q12602346|qid=Q12602346}} estimated to date to the early first half of the Middle Yayoi period; excavated in 1947 from the Katsuma area and owned by Shikaumi Shrine <ref name="銅剣">[http://bunkazai.city.fukuoka.lg.jp/cultural_properties/detail/322 Fragmentary Mold for a Slender Bronze Sword] (Fukuoka City Economic Tourism and Culture Bureau, “Cultural Properties of Fukuoka City”).</ref>. The mold is sandstone; both ends are missing, and the remaining length is 18.1 cm <ref name="銅剣"/>. Designated July 26, 1958 (Shōwa 33).  
* Intangible folk cultural properties  
** Shikaumi Shrine Hosha Festival <ref name="歩射">[http://bunkazai.city.fukuoka.lg.jp/cultural_properties/detail/112 Shikaumi Shrine Hosha Festival] (Fukuoka City Economic Tourism and Culture Bureau, “Cultural Properties of Fukuoka City”).</ref> — Designated March 31, 1959 (Shōwa 34).  
** Yamahome Festival <ref name="山ほめ">[http://bunkazai.city.fukuoka.lg.jp/cultural_properties/detail/115 Yamahome Festival] (Fukuoka City Economic Tourism and Culture Bureau, “Cultural Properties of Fukuoka City”).</ref> — Designated January 12, 1960 (Shōwa 35).  
** Shikaumi Shrine Shinkō Event <ref name="神幸">[http://bunkazai.city.fukuoka.lg.jp/cultural_properties/detail/133 Shikaumi Shrine Shinkō Event] (Fukuoka City Economic Tourism and Culture Bureau, “Cultural Properties of Fukuoka City”).</ref> — Designated August 16, 1960 (Shōwa 35).  

=== Fukuoka City-designated cultural properties ===  
* Tangible cultural properties  
** Illustrated Shikaumi Shrine origin scrolls, 3 hanging scrolls (painting) — Deposited at Fukuoka City Museum. Designated March 7, 1985 (Shōwa 60).  
** Shikaumi Shrine documents, 45 items (books/manuscripts/old texts) — Designated March 7, 1985 (Shōwa 60).  
* Tangible folk cultural property  
** Power stones of Shikaumi Shrine  
**: Edo-period {{ill|Chikaraishi|Q1660393|qid=Q1660393}} beside the shrine worship hall <ref name="力石">[http://bunkazai.city.fukuoka.lg.jp/cultural_properties/detail/427 Power Stones of Shikaumi Shrine] (Fukuoka City Economic Tourism and Culture Bureau, “Cultural Properties of Fukuoka City”).</ref>. A natural basalt stone: length 66 cm, width 36 cm, weight 118.2 kg <ref name="力石"/>. Designated March 2006 (Heisei 18).  

=== Shrine temple (jingūji) ===  
Shikaumi Shrine formerly had a *jingūji* temple called **Kongōzan Kisshōji** <ref name="地名"/>. It is said to have been founded during the {{ill|Eikyō|Q1193059|qid=Q1193059}} era ({{ill|1429|Q6326|qid=Q6326}}–{{ill|1441|Q6402|qid=Q6402}}) <ref name="神々"/>. Originally {{ill|Tiantai|Q668188|qid=Q668188}}, it later changed to {{ill|Zen|Q7953|qid=Q7953}} and became a branch temple of Hakata’s {{ill|Jōten-ji|Q3191242|qid=Q3191242}} <ref name="地名"/>. The temple grounds included a Monju hall and had flourishing devotion to {{ill|Manjushri|Q471696|qid=Q471696|lt=Monju}}, and it is said to have been worshiped as a guardian of seafaring as well <ref name="地名"/>.  

Kisshōji was abolished in March {{ill|Meiji era|Q3125096|qid=Q3125096}} 1 ({{ill|1868|Q7717|qid=Q7717}}) due to the separation of Shinto and Buddhism <ref name="神々"/>. It is thought that Sōgonji, located south of Shikaumi Shrine, inherited Kisshōji’s lineage <ref name="地名"/>. Sōgonji preserves a Heian-period wooden standing Kannon (Fukuoka City-designated tangible cultural property) and a Nanboku-chō-period bronze seated bodhisattva (also Fukuoka City-designated tangible cultural property).
